subject: railgunCarrier
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: six-wheeled railgun carrier braced on stabiliser legs.
Style: low-poly sci-fi military.
reasoning:
I'm planning out the design for a six-wheeled railgun carrier vehicle with deployed outrigger stabiliser legs, roughly 9m long and 3.5m tall, aiming for a substantial but correct code module.

I'm sketching the skeleton structure: chassis root, six wheel joints with front steering, four stabiliser legs with hinge-and-piston joints down to ground pads, and a turret with yaw/pitch/recoil joints for the barrel. I'm deciding whether wheels should hover slightly while the pads rest on the floor to convey the "braced" look, or keep wheels grounded for simplicity.

I'm working out the axle spacing and barrel orientation—placing three axles roughly at z=3.3, 0.6, -0.9 along a long chassis, with the railgun barrel mounted forward over the cab and elevated around 25° for a deployed firing stance, resulting in a quite lengthy overall vehicle.

For the color scheme, I'm leaning toward a sci-fi military aesthetic: dark gunmetal/olive drab hull with hazard-orange stripes and glowing cyan accent rails for the turret platform.

I'm planning to use the clockwork kit's panelled material for hull plating and glow materials for the rails, then sketch out a set of textures—starting with a hazard-stripe pattern for the stabiliser pads and outrigger beams.

I'm listing out the remaining decal ideas: a unit insignia, a "RG-6" label plate, windscreen glass reflection, a "DANGER HV" warning sign, a fire-control glow screen on the turret, cyan energy-coil rings on the barrel, and a rear-bumper chevron stripe. Now I'm sketching the svg() calls to generate these textures at modest sizes.

With the texture list settled, I'm setting up helper functions for box and cylinder geometry, a part-builder wrapper, and mirrored loops for left/right sides. Then I'm starting the main builder for the railgun carrier, working out joint placements: wheel hubs near ground level, frame rails higher up, and the hull deck above that, while deciding which of the six axles get steering joints.

Now I'm defining the wheel joints — steering hinges on Y and spin joints along the axle axis for each side, naming them things like steerL1 and wheelL1 — plus laying out stabilizer outrigger legs at various z-positions relative to the wheel spacing.

I'm reworking the axle spacing and hull layout: three axles around z=2.6/0.6/-1.4, hull spanning roughly 8.8m, turret ring toward the rear, and placing stabilizer pairs near the rear and between axle groups to avoid overlap with the turret mount.

I'm also adding a rear recoil spade with a hydraulic joint, and designing telescopic outrigger beams that slide out from the chassis sides with hydraulic legs lowering to ground pads.

I'll split the outer sleeve joint from the piston/pad joint, marking the piston with a "leg" role so it moves correctly within the chain. Now I'm sketching the cab geometry: a forward cab-over frustum with a raked windscreen sitting above the chassis platform, and I'm defining the chassis frame with lower rails.

Working out the body proportions now — placing the deck/skirt box, sizing the armored side flanks, and figuring out wheel positions so the tires sit just outside the body width without overlapping the hull sides.

Now with outriggers deployed, overall width extends to ±2.9, which works fine. For the turret mount, I'm placing a yaw joint at the rear center for a rotating platform, then adding a pitch joint higher up at the trunnion point angled 22° upward toward the barrel direction, thinking through whether to build the gun parts in the pitch joint's local frame or use explicit direction vectors for each part.

I'll build the gun straight and horizontal in model space first, then apply the pitch rotation at the end using a pose call on the X axis, confirming the sign convention gives the upward tilt I want -- this way everything built gets correctly re-oriented without needing to track rotated coordinates part by part, since I won't need surface queries on the gun anyway.

Working through the geometry, I'm checking that the barrel tip clears the cab roof at the 22° elevation and that the overall silhouette stays reasonable at roughly 7m tall, then laying out the breech housing, cradle sleeve, and rail bars as boxes positioned along the local z-axis relative to the trunnion point.

Now I'm sketching the rest of the gun assembly: insulating spacer blocks with a glowing cyan gap between the rails, tapered side shroud plates alternating tall and short, capacitor drums clustered along the turret sides with glow rings, periodic coil-ring tori around the barrel, and a flared muzzle brake with a glowing tip — planning to build the tapering barrel section as a frustum box.

Writing barrel and turret geometry...

I'm adding a glowing cyan eye lens with screen texture and antenna to the sensor head, treating it as automated rather than crewed. For the turret, I'm placing four capacitor drum cylinders along the rear and sides with a glow effect.

Now I'm working out the drum placement relative to the gun cradle and cheeks, checking the platform width constraints to position the drums just outside the cheek plates, then sizing the drum radius and length to fit on the platform top before moving on to the gun recoil mechanism.

For the recoil, I'm mounting the barrel assembly on a recoil joint that's a child of the pitch joint, aimed along +Z, so posing the pitch rotation at -22 degrees will carry the recoil joint and barrel with it. Then I'm laying out the cab-over-front configuration, figuring out where to place the front axle so it doesn't collide with the cab box, adjusting the front axle z-position and wheel placements accordingly.

Now I'm working through the full z-axis layout: setting axle positions at roughly z=3.0, 1.0, and -1.2, keeping outrigger pads outside the wheel width so they clear physically, placing the mid wheel pair near z=-0.1 and rear pair near z=-3.4, positioning the turret ring and gun trunnion around z=-1.8 to -1.2, and sizing the overall hull from about z=-4.8 to 4.4 with the cab sitting over the front axle between roughly z=1.8 and 4.3.

I'm shaping the cab as an extruded raked profile along z-y, using a windscreen rake from roof down to the front face, extruded with thickness along x, bevelled slightly, then planning a windscreen glass plane oriented to match the raked front face's normal direction.

I'm also sketching side window planes near x=±1.21 and door insignia decals, continuing to describe these as flat textured planes placed on the cab's side faces.

Now I'm adding cab details: a roof hatch, light bar, glowing headlights, grille vents, front bumper with tow hooks and winch, armored chevron plating, mirrors, an exhaust stack, a snorkel intake, and a roof cupola with sensor dome and searchlight. I'm also positioning the front grille panel and headlight glow slits at the front fascia plane.

For the hull, I'm laying out a long paneled main deck box spanning the chassis length, then figuring out where side lockers can fit between wheel gaps without colliding with the tires -- checking tire radius and axle spacing to find the small gap between the second and third axles where a mid locker or outrigger mount could go.

Then I move to the rear section behind the last axle, placing rear outriggers at a wider stance, adding mudflaps near the fenders, and sketching in a rear hinged spade plate at the very back of the frame.

I shape the spade plate at an angle so it sits low near the ground without actually poking through the floor, keeping it just above zero height. I also plan the rear detailing with tail lights and an under-run bar, then shift to thinking about the wheels, going with a faceted cylinder tire shape plus separate tread blocks rather than a full lathe geometry.

For the six wheels, I decide to build each one from a tire, hub, tread blocks, and lug nuts, and since parts are limited I plan to merge the tread geometry per wheel into a single mesh rather than adding dozens of tiny parts. I'll write a reusable function that generates a fresh wheel geometry each time it's called, since reusing the same geometry object across multiple parts risks unwanted mutation when the builder applies transforms.

Writing tire geometry...

Lug nuts merged into one piece, cap as another, totaling roughly 24 parts across four wheels. Skipping decals for simplicity, I'm moving to axles and suspension, planning an axle beam box running along the x-axis.

I'll wire wheel hubs to the chassis with the diff pumpkin, leaf-spring boxes, and hydraulic struts attached, letting steering axles pivot while ignoring bounce physics, and parenting wheel joints to the chassis with spin-joint bones for the wheel parts themselves. For armor detailing, I'm planning hazard stripe texture along the hull skirts, a "RG-6" stencil and star emblem on the cab door, and a unit badge on the turret cheek.

For the paint scheme, I'm settling on a low-poly military sci-fi palette: desaturated sage base, amber accent, dark shadows, and a cyan glow, applying a mottled camo pattern with panel overlays, then calculating a low texel density since the vehicle's surface area is so large.

Checking the math at 2048px paint size I get roughly 8mm per texel, which risks losing fine panel seams and rivets—so I'm planning to write a custom paint function with wider seam lines (around 1.8cm) to stay visible, and limiting detailed painting to the hull, cab, and turret rather than every small part.

Writing camo paint function...

Still writing seam and lighting logic...

For materials, I'll reuse the clockwork kit's metal presets like iron and steel for rails and gun parts, and consider a blued-steel look for the railgun rails to pair with a cyan glow. Then I'm planning the SVG texture set, starting with a hazard stripe pattern for pad edges and beam caps.

For geometry mapping, cylinders wrap the texture around the sides via UV coordinates, so hazard stripes on pad rims would read as chevrons with matching stripes on the caps — a good hazard-pad effect. Next I'm sketching an emblem texture, a unit insignia with a star and wing or rail motifs, for use on other parts.

Beyond that I'm planning several more texture types: a stencil decal with text like "RAILGUN-6," a dark blue windshield glass with reflection streaks, small side windows, a glowing fire-control screen with cyan reticle and "CHARGE 87%" text, a yellow warning triangle reading "DANGER — HV 40MJ" for the capacitor area, and a red/white hazard variant for the rear bumper chevrons.

I'm also considering kill-mark rings as a texture band near the barrel muzzle, while skipping radar dish patterns and headlights as unnecessary. For implementation, I'll use the texture parameter on part calls so textures render their own colors, apply glow only to textured or flat surfaces (like the screen), and place decal planes slightly offset from the flat hull box surfaces.

Writing builder helpers...

Working through the cross products to figure out which way local axes map when viewed from the +X side, to determine if the drawn text would appear mirrored to the viewer.

I verify the front, rear, and raked plane orientations all check out consistently with the viewer-facing convention. Now I'm setting up the concrete constants for the cab geometry—radius, hub height, width, and other dimensions to build out the full coordinate layout.

Still placing frame rails...

I'll simplify by keeping axle rods, a diff sphere, slanted shock rods, and a leaf spring box per axle, with the first two axles steering for that 6x6-ish feel. Then I'm adding a central drive shaft rod running along z and starting on the underbelly plate for the hull.

Now I'm sketching the main hull body dimensions and position, then adding wheel fenders with top panels, outward flare lips, and angled mud flaps for the rear wheels.

Working out fender clearance above the tyre and checking overlap with the deck sides, then moving to the cab's extruded profile shape defined by a series of z,y coordinate points.

Now I'm computing the raked windscreen plane — its direction vector, center position, and offset from the cab body, sizing it to roughly 2.1 wide by 1.0 tall with small bevels and camo paint coloring for the cab.

I still need to add an armored brow/visor plate above the windscreen and side windows — placing a tilted slanted box over the glass, then sizing and positioning rectangular window planes on each side face of the cab around z 2.8–3.3.

For the doors, I'm adding thin dark seam outlines using a helper that draws rectangle borders, plus a door handle box and an emblem plane placed lower on the door panel.

For stencils, I'm positioning a "RG-6" marking along the deck flank near the rear, sizing and placing it between the wheels and stabilizer beams so it sits clear of other geometry, then considering a locker placement near the mid-deck area.

Now I'm designing the cab roof details—a hatch cylinder, sensor turret, amber light bar, antennas, and roof rack—then moving to the front end with a grille panel with slat boxes, headlights with glowing lenses, and a bumper, all positioned relative to the nose's front face.

I'm adding hazard stripe texturing on the bumper front, a winch drum centered inside the bumper with a fairlead roller cutout, and small tow hooks as rods or tori, then sketching the cab's rear bulkhead with an exhaust stack mounted on the right side.

Now I'm placing a snorkel on the left with an elbow bend, roof-mounted items like a glowing light bar, a hatch, an antenna whip with a ball tip, and an IFF sensor dome, then starting to figure out what equipment sits on the deck between the turret and cab.

I'm sketching a power module box with vented grilles, cooling fans, an indicator light and warning sign, plus coolant tanks, while checking that it fits between the turret ring and deck top without colliding with the gun barrel's elevated resting angle.

I'm skipping a stowed barrel-rest fork since the gun's elevation would leave it floating awkwardly, and instead moving on to defining the turret's internal construction, starting with the yaw joint's pivot location and orientation.

Now I'm laying out the slew ring and rotating platform geometry -- a static ring bonded to the chassis with a bolted torus detail, and a separate rotating platform box sized and positioned to sit on top of it.

I'm sketching a sloped front glacis armor wedge profile for the platform using an extruded side-view outline, considering whether to use a frustum shape or a simple extrude.

Then I'm defining the side cheeks as an extruded triangular profile with coordinates forming the trunnion mount area, checking the inner gap clearance against the gun's half-width and positioning the trunnion point in the side plane.

Checking the gun's rotation about the trunnion, I realize the breech end drops too low when pitched up, colliding with the platform top. I need to raise the trunnion height and shorten the breech's backward extent to keep clearance.

Now I'm working out the elevation ram geometry as a two-part cylinder-piston linkage: the cylinder base mounts on the yaw bone while the piston extends toward the gun's pitch attachment point, so rotation of the pitch bone about the trunnion needs to move that attachment correctly to keep the ram visually connected across poses.

Let me try attaching the ram further forward on the cradle underside instead, ahead of the trunnion, and recompute the rotated position—that places it just outside the cheeks, so I need to find a ram base point on the platform that works geometrically with this new attachment.

But I realize the real issue is the pre-pose vs post-pose coordinate problem: if I build the piston geometry using the rest-pose attachment point and then rotate the trunnion bone, the piston's end won't actually track the moving attachment point correctly, so the ram will visually disconnect. I need to actually trace through how the rig handles this.

Writing helper function logic...

Working out the quaternion math for the rotation...

Similarly for the barrel cylinders I'll use the same `gcyl` helper aligned along the direction vector. The cab and turret cheeks stay unposed since turret yaw is zero, and I'm setting up the recoil bone joint at the trunnion offset along the barrel direction, parented to the pitch joint.

Now I'm computing the elevation ram geometry—finding the attach point on the cradle underside relative to the trunnion, verifying the base-to-attach distance comes out to about 1.03, and splitting the ram into cylinder and piston segments bound to yaw and pitch respectively. I'm placing twin rams symmetrically at x=±0.35 to fit under the gun between the cheeks, then sizing the cradle housing box around the trunnion.

I'm laying out the trunnion pins and rounded end caps on the cheeks, then defining the gun's internal components in local barrel coordinates: the breech block as a metal box with rear capacitor cable connectors, and the cradle sleeve as a long metal box with panel detailing further down the barrel.

Now I'm shaping the barrel shroud as a tapered frustum narrowing toward the muzzle, then reconsidering the design to expose twin rails with insulator spacers and a glowing bore for a more distinctive railgun look rather than fully enclosing the barrel.

Placing the rails symmetrically on either side of the bore with a visible gap between them, filling that gap with a cyan glow strip running most of the barrel's length to suggest the energized rail channel.

Along the length I'm adding periodic clamp/sleeve blocks to look like structural insulators holding the rails together, plus considering torus rings or rectangular tie-frames spaced every ~1.1 meters for mechanical bracing.

Adding zig-zag diagonal rods between the lower spine and rail bottoms, then designing the muzzle end cap with a flared ring, glowing cyan tip plate, and sensor details. I'm also working out how to orient the side texture planes on the cradle so they follow the barrel's slope using proper quaternion rotation.

Now I'm placing capacitor bank drums in the turret along the yaw bone, sized and positioned on either side of the platform.

I'm adding glow-band tori and strap details around each drum, then routing catmull sweep cables from the drum rear ends back to the gun breech position, accounting for how the cables need to clear the cheek geometry as the gun rotates.

I'll simplify by routing the cables from the drum ends behind the cheeks curving toward the breech, keeping precise pivot offsets loose since they're mostly visual. I might add a rear bustle box to the turret to anchor where the cables terminate, then render them as dark rubber sweeps following the bone yaw from the drums.

Then I'm planning the turret extras: a sensor mast and fire-control pod on the platform front with a glowing lens cylinder, plus a rear equipment cabinet holding a gunner display screen plane positioned at the back bustle.

I'm also placing a warning triangle and emblem on the cheek outer faces, positioning them above the drum tops so they're clear of the curved drum geometry, with coordinates worked out for both the emblem and warning sign sizes and placements.

Now I'm adding details to the other turret: a radar dish mounted on a post at the rear, four tilted smoke discharger tubes on the front cheeks, and a power module on the deck with a boxy base, louvred top slats, and side fan grilles rendered as circular discs.

I'm fleshing out the fan assemblies with cylindrical housings and thin blade boxes, plus exhaust stacks with rain caps, a front coolant radiator, and a small glowing indicator strip on top. I'm also adding tool lockers, jerry cans, pioneer tools like shovels on the flanks, and a rolled camo net on the rear deck.

Now I'm designing the rear spade/stabilizer assembly: a hinged arm joint descending at an angle from the deck, connected by hydraulic struts to a tilted blade-shaped plate, along with rear tail lights and a license plate mount.

Figuring out the spade's tilt direction so the bottom digs backward relative to the top, and setting the rotation axis accordingly. I'm also planning stiffener ribs, a hazard stripe band, hydraulic struts connecting the deck bracket to the plate, and a pivot joint for the spade at the chassis.

Now I'm working out the outrigger legs: four total, two per side, each with a hinge joint at the chassis and a telescoping beam extending outward with a downward-angled direction, modeling fixed housing boxes plus sliding inner beams for the deployed stabilizer legs.

Still defining leg geometry...

I should also add hazard stripes on the slide beam end cap and a small amber warning light near the top of the leg. Pads need to stay flush with the ground at y=0, so I'll skip spikes that would penetrate the floor, and I'm also planning out mirror arms, door handles, and side skirt plates under the deck between the wheels.

I'm settling on ten textures total (HAZARD square, HAZSTRIP long, EMBLEM, STENCIL, SCREEN, WARN, WINDSHIELD, SIDEWIN, KILLS, REDCHEV), using a larger size for the stencil text for readability. Writing SVG code...

Drawing the emblem geometry...

Now I'm thinking through a vehicle callsign stencil, maybe "HAMMERFALL" with a unit designation subtitle, rendered in a bold monospace stencil font for flavor.

Next I'm designing the targeting screen with a dark teal background, cyan grid lines, a reticle and crosshair, a charge bar graph, and status text like "CHG 87%" and "ARMED," plus a warning icon—a yellow triangle with a black lightning bolt and "40MJ" label—and finally a windshield panel with a dark teal gradient and faint diagonal reflection streaks.

Now I'm sketching the side window pane, kill marker rings (white rings with red centers drawn in a loop), and red/white chevron patterns for the rear bumper using a generated polygon loop, before moving on to defining the paint colors at the module level.

Setting up the color palette constants and planning the hull paint object, which I'll generate from a single consistent seed so the camo pattern flows continuously across the cab, hull, turret, and power module parts.

I'm also sketching out the metal finishes for iron, steel, and blued surfaces, plus a weathered tire paint that mixes rubber with dust buildup near the bottom using noise-weighted smoothstep blending.

Checking that total painted area across hull, tyres, and gun stays within texture resolution limits so camo noise and seam widths remain sharp enough at 2048px, and flagging flat shading for cylindrical parts. Now writing the hull paint function...

Writing color blending logic...

Adding rivet highlights...then lighting with warm top tint and dirt/dust accumulation based on vertical position and noise.

I also want paint chip scratches using high-frequency noise mapped to a brown metal tone, and I need to double-check all the needed functions—noise, mix, rgb, smoothstep, paint—are exported from the single SDK module, pulling in the clockwork kit for anything metal-specific.

Settling on the `Fill` type imported from the builder package for color parameters, since both the kit and the color helper share that type, so I'll keep typing consistent across the sampler functions.

Defining part option types and a wrapper helper...

Writing helper function and imports...

I'm importing the clockwork metal kit and glow effects plus a geometry merging utility, then setting up the meta export with the ship's name and description, followed by constants and a color palette, with texture definitions placed inside the build function.

For the skeleton, I'm sketching out the build function's structure, starting with a chassis joint as the spine, then looping over both sides to create steering hinges and wheel hubs at calculated axle positions, with parent joints connecting the hierarchy for the first two wheel rows.

Adding outrigger and stabiliser leg joints...

Building the stabiliser leg chain...

Now I'm defining the turret joints: yaw at the trunnion base pointing up, pitch at the trunnion, and recoil along the gun axis, all parented in sequence as hinges, with rams as separate unjointed pieces. I'm also adding the spade joint and the left/right cooling fan joints on the power module sides.

For hatches, I'm planning a roof hatch lid hinged at the back edge of the cab, plus left/right door hinge joints carrying door panels that combine a lower body panel with a framed window section cut from thin boxes and a window plane.

I'm working out the hinge geometry so the door and window align with the sloped roof profile, computing where the door top and window edges fall against the slope at different z positions, then moving on to actually writing the geometry generation functions.

Now I'm building the tire geometry: a cylindrical carcass with tread blocks arranged radially around it. I'm positioning each block by rotating around the Y axis so its radial face points outward at the tire's radius, computing the block's tangential, width, and depth dimensions and its placement in local cylinder coordinates.

I add a chevron effect by tilting each block about its radial axis, with the sign flipped per side to create a herringbone pattern, then merging all the geometries since they share the same vertex attributes. The total triangle count stays manageable across all six wheels, and I'm skipping the sidewall bulge detail for now to keep things simple.

Now I'm structuring the wheel assembly: a tyre at the hub, a rim barrel using a short cylinder, plus a hub cap offset toward the outer face along the axle direction so the hub detailing appears on the correct side per wheel.

Keeping rim color dark, lugs steel-colored, cap amber, and skipping the inner wheel face for now — that's 5 parts per wheel times 6 wheels, 30 total. For the axle setup, I'm attaching an axle rod to the chassis per wheel and adding a steering knuckle box at the steer joint, keeping tie rods and brake discs out of scope for simplicity.

Now I'm working out the hub-to-wheel gap, placing a differential sphere flat on the chassis per axle, stacking leaf-spring boxes and shock rods with coil sleeves on each side, and planning drive shaft rods and frame rails before assembling the full deck. I also want to nail down the lighting scheme: amber-white glowing headlights, an amber beacon on the cab roof, red glowing tail lights, amber warning lights on the outriggers, and green indicators.

I'm sketching the cab body as an extruded profile with a tall windshield rake, tracing the outline points from the base up through the roofline and down the front slope, checking that the path doesn't self-intersect and that bevels on the corners look right before finalizing the extrusion parameters.

Now I'm placing the windshield plane on that rake face, computing its center and normal offset so it sits flush against the beveled surface, and sizing it to fit within the rake length. I'm also considering adding a thin armored visor brow above it for detail.

Adding front fascia details...

I'm adding small torus tow hooks, skipping headlight guards, and realizing the step placement conflicts with the front wheel position -- I need to reconsider the cab-over layout so the door step doesn't collide with the front tire arch.

Working through the cab fender geometry now, checking that the fender flare and door bottom clear each other properly, then moving on to defining the roof hatch hinge joint.

Adding roof details...

Adding mirror support rods with dark glass, then building the hull deck: a main box chassis, a non-slip top plate, raised side rails, and locker boxes along the sides.

Shrinking fenders to 1.4 length gives better clearance gaps, and the locker fits cleanly between them with the outrigger housing tucked below. Now I'm moving to the rear section of the chassis, placing the rear outrigger at z=-3.4 and designing the rear face with glowing taillights, a license plate, and an underrun bumper bar.

I'm rethinking the rear bumper layout since the spade arm's plate overlaps it -- deciding to skip the standard bumper and instead put taillights, hazard plates, and a REDCHEV stripe directly on the rear panel, with the spade sized at 2.3 width. I'm also positioning hydraulic strut rods running from the top of the spade down to its rear plate to visually support it.

Still placing hinge struts and ribs...

I'll skip the hazard strip and tooth-spike details to avoid floor penetration, opting instead for a simple cutting-edge bar along the bottom, and confirm the plate's bottom corner height stays safely above the floor clearance.

Now I'm designing the power module block above the deck, with roof louvre slats and side fan intakes featuring circular grilles, spokes, a fan joint, and blade geometry on each side.

Adding fan blades and guard rings, then placing twin exhaust stacks with conical caps on top plus coolant piping, and considering a warning sign plane for the module's rear face.

I'm repositioning the warning sign to the module's side faces instead, then adding armored cable conduits that arc from the module to the turret's slew ring with some slack, and starting on rear deck equipment like a net roll cylinder.

I'm also roughing out ammo crates with amber stripes, jerry cans, and considering a rack of long projectile canisters for the railgun magazine behind the turret platform on the rear deck.

Now I'm adding the sloped glacis armor to the turret platform front, then placing a rear bustle box behind it on the platform, working through the exact z-boundaries so the bustle sits flush against the platform edge without overlapping the drums.

I'm also planning the rear bustle screen panel with a glow effect, side ventilation louvres, and cable entry points, then simplifying the drum cabling to short runs connecting the drums to the bustle sides and the bustle front to the breech rear rather than one long cable run.

I'm computing the transformed breech position so the cable connects from the bustle to a point near the breech that stays rigid along the yaw axis but keeps a short, slack-looking run between the cheeks, confirming it clears them since the cable sits within the cheek spacing.

Now I'm sizing the drum to fit between the cheeks with minor overlap, then placing turret-top sensor gear — a sensor pod on one cheek, an EO sensor and radar dish at the bustle, and a sensor mast with a ball sensor on top.

Adding smoke dischargers at the platform's front corners, angling three tubes outward at each side with caps, and finishing the muzzle brake framing at the barrel tip.

Checking barrel dimensions so the muzzle tip lands correctly, then setting glow intensities for the rail strips versus other emissive parts. I'm also placing kill marks on the cradle sides as thin rectangular decals sized to match the texture's aspect ratio.

I'm working out the quaternion rotations needed to orient the text planes on each side of the gun so they read correctly relative to the viewer, and considering whether to add an emblem to the cradle cheeks, adjusting the sleeve box dimensions so the side decal planes sit flush against the cradle surface.

For recoil, I'm placing the barrel assembly components—rails, clamps, truss, muzzle, glow—further down the bone, along with the cradle sleeve and breech on the pitch joint, plus two recoil buffer cylinders mounted on the cradle sides with piston rods feeding into the barrel assembly. Now I'm tallying up the expected part count across wheels, axles, frame, cab, hull, turret, gun, outriggers, spade, and power systems—landing around 490 parts, which exceeds my target range but stays well under the 1000 limit, so I'm fine moving forward to write the actual code.

Writing helper functions for the pitch-angle geometry...

Defining helper geometry functions for cylinders, tori, and rods...

Now I'm setting up type definitions and utility functions for angles and colors, then starting on the color palette...

Writing paint functions for hull texture...

I'm defining deck plating and metal materials for different parts—iron, steel, blued finishes—then weighing whether painting many small rod pieces individually will bloat the texture atlas with excessive chart tiles relative to their actual surface area.

Given the atlas resolution limits, I decide to use flat colors for small bits like rods and bolts, reserving the paint() function for larger surfaces like the hull, cab, and gun components. Now I'm starting to write the actual build function...

Setting up builder config...

Generating texture definitions...

Writing SVG chevron patterns...

Planning the joint hierarchy, starting with the chassis as root before attaching the wheels.

Defining wheel assembly logic...

Adding the ball joint sphere and reinforcing rib gussets, then setting up the stabilizer-piston-pad joint chain with a polyline path and sleeve box geometry...

Adding housing, hazard cap, and brace geometry...

Now I'm adding the sloped brace rod connecting the housing to the sleeve, tying it to the slide bone since the sleeve moves with the stabilizer. I'll parent the chain to the slide joint, add an amber warning beacon glowing on top of the sleeve, and skip the front towing tools detail for now.

Next I'm laying out the door assembly: hinge joints on left and right doors parented to the chassis, with panel boxes, window frame geometry, a window plane, handle, and emblem positioned around the door region.

Still placing door trim pieces, then checking the painted hull color and window plane orientation for each side; I'm also figuring out an emblem placement on the door panel and a stencil decal near the outrigger housing on the deck flank.

I'm positioning hazard stripe decals along the flank and bumper, sketching the gun struts and skipping ladder steps, and adding small glowing indicator lights on the drums before assembling the gun parts onto the cradle, breech, and recoil bones.

Now I'm placing the breech box, rear cap with capacitor lugs, and cradle sleeve on the pitch bone, sizing the sleeve to fit within the breech without overlap, then setting up the trunnion pin rods.

Still adding geometry... trunnion caps, cheek bushings, sleeve bolt rows, a glowing charge indicator light, and panel line bands around the sleeve.

Now I'm placing kill marks, recoil buffers, and piston rods on the recoil bone, then building out the shroud root and rail geometry for the barrel group.

For the rails, I'm sizing them to run the length of the barrel with a bit of flush at the tip, painted in blued metal, and adding a glowing cyan strip recessed slightly in the gap between them to suggest an energy channel. I'm skipping separate insulator spacers since the glow fills that space, and now adding clamp frames further down the shaft.

Writing clamp frame boxes...

Still designing truss and muzzle geometry...

Adding a turret floodlight, confirming no collisions overall, then moving into writing the actual build code with helper functions for blocks and cylinders attached to bones.

I'm checking that glow works on textured planes since Part exposes a mesh, and confirming that rod and sweep outputs are also glow-compatible. Now I'm setting up the hull paint function and importing geometry merging utilities for the tyre, then moving on to building the lug geometry.
